title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

SecurityEvent

CVE-2026-0257 GlobalProtect VPN session from Qilin affiliate source IPs AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful VPN/network authentications originating from the specific source IPs Arctic Wolf attributed to Qilin affiliates exploiting the PAN-OS GlobalProtect auth-bypass (CVE-2026-0257). Article-specific because it pivots on the confirmed exploitation infrastructure rather than a generic VPN-anomaly. Rationale: Anchored on the five VPN source IPs Arctic Wolf explicitly published (108.61.229.217, 108.61.75.232, 2.188.33.52, 199.247.22.193, 70.34.205.43) plus the wider campaign IOC set; these are second-source confirmed exploitation infrastructure, not article-only claims. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/exploitation-of-cve-2026-0257-leads-to-qilin-ransomware/ • https://security.paloaltonetworks.com/CVE-2026-0257 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-globalprotect-vpn-bug-now-exploited-in-ransomware-attacks/

NTDS.dit theft via ntdsutil IFM to C:\Windows\Temp\NTDS AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the exact ntdsutil Install-From-Media command Qilin affiliates used to dump Active Directory (NTDS.dit) after VPN access: 'ntdsutil activate instance ntds ifm create full C:\Windows\Temp\NTDS'. High-fidelity because legitimate IFM to a Temp directory is near-zero. Rationale: Uses the verbatim ntdsutil IFM command line from Arctic Wolf's report ('ifm create full C:\Windows\Temp\NTDS'); IFM to Temp is an unambiguous AD-dumping signal distinct from routine DC maintenance. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/exploitation-of-cve-2026-0257-leads-to-qilin-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1003.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DC administrator legitimately creating an IFM media set to build a new domain controller (usually to a dedicated path, not Temp)
  • Backup/DR tooling that snapshots NTDS via ntdsutil
  • Microsoft support-guided AD recovery procedures
  • Automation building read-only domain controllers
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Windows\Temp\", @"\PerfLogs\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a domain controller and whether the initiating account/parent process is a known DC-admin workflow; inspect the target path (C:\Windows\Temp\NTDS is malicious). 2) Contain: isolate the DC, kill the process, and treat all domain credentials as compromised — begin krbtgt double-reset planning. 3) Hunt: search for exfil of the NTDS/SYSTEM hive (rclone, MEGA, admin-share copies to \\host\c$\Windows\Temp) and for the comsvcs LSASS dump on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "ntdsutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "ifm" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\ntdsutil.exe"
| where CommandLine has "ifm" and CommandLine has "create"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LSASS dump via rundll32 comsvcs.dll MiniDump to output.odt AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Qilin's LSASS credential dump: rundll32 invoking comsvcs.dll MiniDump with output written to a disguised .odt file in C:\Windows\Temp. Distinct from generic LSASS-handle rules — this pivots on the specific LOLBIN command line and the .odt masquerade. Rationale: Uses the exact comsvcs.dll MiniDump command line documented by Arctic Wolf including the disguised C:\Windows\Temp\output.odt sink; the LOLBIN + MiniDump keyword pair is a process-creation signal separate from generic LSASS-access telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/exploitation-of-cve-2026-0257-leads-to-qilin-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1003.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate crash-dump troubleshooting that happens to use comsvcs MiniDump (rare, usually not to .odt/Temp)
  • EDR or DFIR tooling invoking comsvcs for memory capture during an authorized IR
  • Developer/QA memory-dump automation
  • Microsoft support scripts collecting process dumps
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full command line for the target PID (is it lsass?) and the output path (.odt or Temp = malicious); check parent process and initiating account. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill rundll32, delete the dump file, and reset credentials for every account logged onto that host. 3) Hunt: look for the dump being staged/exfiltrated (rclone.exe, MEGA, admin-share copies) and for ntdsutil IFM on domain controllers reached from the same account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "comsvcs.dll" and ProcessCommandLine has "MiniDump"
| extend SuspiciousOutput = ProcessCommandLine has ".odt" or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Windows\Temp\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, SuspiciousOutput, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe"
| where CommandLine has "comsvcs.dll" and CommandLine has "MiniDump"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Qilin ransomware payload C:\PerfLogs\win.exe with --no-admin/--password flags AIInstallation High
Detects execution of the Qilin encryptor from its staging directory C:\PerfLogs\win.exe using its distinctive password-gated, UAC-suppressing flags (--password / --no-admin). Article-specific to this campaign's binary path and CLI. Rationale: Combines the campaign's exact staging path (C:\PerfLogs\win.exe) with the documented '--password' and '--no-admin' encryptor flags from Arctic Wolf; both the PerfLogs directory for an EXE and those flags are individually anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/exploitation-of-cve-2026-0257-leads-to-qilin-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1486 T1548
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign in-house utility literally named win.exe run with unrelated arguments
  • Performance-diagnostic tooling that legitimately writes to C:\PerfLogs
  • Software installer temporarily staging a helper named win.exe
  • Security-team detonation of the sample in a sandbox
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the SHA256 and full command line, confirm the parent (often PsExec/NetExec or a scheduled task) and whether encryption artifacts (renamed files, ransom note) already exist. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, kill the process tree, and network-quarantine any host that ran the same hash to stop domain-wide spread. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts with C:\PerfLogs\win.exe or the Run-key persistence, check for prior shadow-copy/Veeam deletion, and validate backups are intact and offline.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has @"\PerfLogs\" and FileName =~ "win.exe")
     or (FileName =~ "win.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--no-admin","--password"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688

Qilin Run-key persistence pointing to C:\PerfLogs\win.exe AIInstallation High
Detects the autostart Run-key value Qilin affiliates created (a random 6-lowercase-char value name) pointing at the encryptor in C:\PerfLogs\win.exe. Pivots on the payload path in registry value data, which is the durable persistence artifact. Rationale: Anchors on the payload path (PerfLogs\win.exe) appearing as Run-key value data, the persistence artifact Arctic Wolf tied to the random 6-char value-name pattern; a Run key launching an EXE from PerfLogs is inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/exploitation-of-cve-2026-0257-leads-to-qilin-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named diagnostic tool installed under PerfLogs adding a startup entry (very rare)
  • Backup/monitoring agent misconfigured to stage under PerfLogs
  • Security tooling writing a decoy Run key during testing
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the value name/data and the initiating process/account that wrote the key; correlate with any C:\PerfLogs\win.exe execution on the host. 2) Contain: delete the Run-key value, isolate the host, and disable the account that created it. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for Run keys whose data references \PerfLogs\ and for the same random-6-char naming pattern across other autostart locations and MeshUserTask scheduled tasks.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has @"\PerfLogs\" and RegistryValueData has "win.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has @"\PerfLogs\" and RegistryValueData has "win.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rclone exfiltration to MEGA from C:\Windows\Temp\rclone.exe (double-extortion) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the pre-encryption data theft stage: Qilin affiliates ran rclone from C:\Windows\Temp to push data to MEGA cloud. Pivots on rclone in Temp plus mega/copy/sync flags, article-specific to the double-extortion tradecraft described. Rationale: Uses the documented exfil tooling (rclone at C:\Windows\Temp\rclone.exe) and MEGA destination from Arctic Wolf; rclone in Temp with cloud-sync flags is a strong staging-then-exfil indicator preceding encryption. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/exploitation-of-cve-2026-0257-leads-to-qilin-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1048
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin using rclone for legitimate cloud backups (usually from Program Files, not Temp)
  • Developer syncing artifacts to a personal cloud remote
  • Backup software bundling rclone in a signed install path
  • Red-team exfil simulation
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has @"\Windows\Temp\" or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the rclone command line for the remote/bucket and config path, and correlate DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound volume to MEGA endpoints from the same host. 2) Contain: kill the process, block MEGA domains/IPs at egress, and isolate the host to stop further exfil. 3) Hunt: identify which file servers/DCs the account touched, estimate exfil scope from network byte counts, and check for the follow-on encryptor (PerfLogs\win.exe) — exfil here precedes encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "rclone.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\Windows\Temp\" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mega","copy","sync","--config")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rclone.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("mega","copy","sync","--config") or NewProcessName has "\\Windows\\Temp\\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Qilin inhibit-recovery: shadow copy, backup-catalog and Veeam deletion AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the pre-encryption recovery-destruction stage: vssadmin/wbadmin/bcdedit removing shadow copies and boot recovery, plus Veeam backup infrastructure deletion that Arctic Wolf flagged as a Qilin behaviour. Scoped to non-machine accounts to keep FPs low. Rationale: Combines standard inhibit-recovery LOLBINs with the campaign-specific Veeam backup-deletion behaviour Arctic Wolf attributed to Qilin; the Veeam clause and non-machine-account scope raise fidelity above a generic vssadmin rule. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/exploitation-of-cve-2026-0257-leads-to-qilin-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam backup jobs performing legitimate pre-snapshot cleanup
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting VSS or resizing shadow storage with vssadmin
  • Windows imaging/DISM or backup-rotation scripts calling wbadmin delete
  • Disaster-recovery testing that resets bcdedit recovery flags
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Veeam.Backup.Manager.exe","Veeam.Backup.Shell.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !=~ "services.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating account/parent process — a user or PsExec/NetExec parent (not the Veeam service) deleting Veeam backups is malicious; check timing relative to any encryptor execution. 2) Contain: isolate the host, verify offline/immutable backups are intact, and freeze backup infrastructure credentials. 3) Hunt: look on the same and neighbouring hosts for PerfLogs\win.exe, rclone exfil, and ntdsutil dumps — recovery destruction typically fires minutes before mass encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "delete" and ProcessCommandLine has "shadows")
     or (FileName =~ "wbadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "delete")
     or (FileName =~ "bcdedit.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "recoveryenabled" and ProcessCommandLine has "no")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "Veeam" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Stop-Service","delete","sc "))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\vssadmin.exe" and CommandLine has "delete" and CommandLine has "shadows")
     or (NewProcessName endswith "\\wbadmin.exe" and CommandLine has "delete")
     or (NewProcessName endswith "\\bcdedit.exe" and CommandLine has "recoveryenabled" and CommandLine has "no")
     or (CommandLine has "Veeam" and (CommandLine has "Stop-Service" or CommandLine has "delete"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Qilin RMM/tunneling tools (Ngrok, AnyDesk, MeshAgent) staged in PerfLogs/Temp AICommand & Control Medium
Detects unauthorized remote-access and tunneling tools Qilin affiliates dropped into staging directories (C:\PerfLogs, C:\Windows\Temp, C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk) for persistence and C2, including the \MeshUserTask scheduled task. Pivots on the tool names in anomalous paths. Rationale: Uses the specific RMM/tunneler set and anomalous drop paths (Ngrok, AnyDesk in PerfLogs/Temp/ProgramData, MeshAgent + \MeshUserTask) documented by Arctic Wolf; scoping AnyDesk to staging dirs avoids sanctioned-AnyDesk noise. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/exploitation-of-cve-2026-0257-leads-to-qilin-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1219 T1572 T1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT department sanctioned AnyDesk installed in the standard Program Files path (excluded by the staging-dir scope)
  • Developers legitimately using ngrok to expose a local dev service
  • MeshCentral used as an approved remote-management platform
  • Portable RMM run from Temp during a legitimate helpdesk session
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "anydesk.exe" and FolderPath has @"\Program Files (x86)\AnyDesk\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the tool is unsanctioned on this host, capture the ngrok tunnel token/AnyDesk ID and the MeshUserTask definition, and check outbound connections the tool established. 2) Contain: kill the process, remove the scheduled task and dropped binaries, block the tunneling domains at egress, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: enumerate the fleet for the same tools in PerfLogs/Temp and for \MeshUserTask, and correlate with the VPN entry account and PerfLogs\win.exe execution to scope the intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "ngrok.exe")
     or (FileName =~ "anydesk.exe" and FolderPath has_any (@"\PerfLogs\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\AnyDesk\"))
     or (FileName has "MeshAgent")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "MeshUserTask")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\ngrok.exe")
     or (NewProcessName endswith "\\anydesk.exe" and (NewProcessName has "\\PerfLogs\\" or NewProcessName has "\\Windows\\Temp\\" or NewProcessName has "\\ProgramData\\AnyDesk\\"))
     or (NewProcessName has "MeshAgent")
     or (CommandLine has "MeshUserTask")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs

| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f") or SHA1 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f") or MD5 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f") or SHA1 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f") or MD5 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New Project CAV3RN module abuses Outlook calendar events for C2 and DNS AAAA records for configuration recovery

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-21 9 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Kaspersky GReAT experts describe a new Project CAV3RN C2 module. It uses Outlook calendar for communication via Microsoft Graph and has a backup connection via DNS AAAA responses.

ATT&CKT1190 T1528

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — New Project CAV3RN module abuses Outlook calendar events for C2 and DNS AAAA rec
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CAV3RN AzureCommunication.dll config file 'logAzure.txt' written to disk · [LLM] CAV3RN framework module DLLs loaded/dropped (AzureCommunication / n-HTCommp / masqueraded uxtheme) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] CAV3RN/HOLLOWGRAPH DNS AAAA config-recovery beaconing to cloudlanecdn[.]com · [LLM] Anomalous DLL-host process reaching Microsoft Graph/login.microsoftonline for calendar C2 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
CAV3RN/HOLLOWGRAPH DNS AAAA config-recovery beaconing to cloudlanecdn[.]com AICommand & Control High
Hunts the DNS-based fallback channel AzureCommunication.dll uses when Microsoft Graph auth fails: AAAA queries to actor-controlled cloudlanecdn.com and its subdomains, which encode configuration fragments (tenant ID, client ID/secret, mailbox) inside IPv6 answers. The .p. (probe length) and .q. (retrieve) label structure and long hex data labels are unique to this module. Rationale: Anchored on the confirmed C2 domain cloudlanecdn.com plus the AAAA query type and the .p./.q. label structure documented in the article (example d.53466d4c67515a.0.p.cloudlanecdn.com); cross-checked against Group-IB and Check Point who both cite cloudlanecdn.com as actor infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/cavern-manticore-exposing-iran-linked-modular-c2-framework/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowgraph-malware-hides-c2-and-stolen.html
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1132.001 T1008
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately registered internal service that happens to share the cloudlanecdn.com string (none known — domain is exclusively malicious)
  • Security scanners / DNS sinkholes actively resolving the IOC domain for research
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling pre-resolving IOC feeds
  • Passive DNS mirroring appliances replaying the query
Suppression filter
| where not(Computer has_any ("sinkhole","ti-enrich","dns-research"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the querying host and the process that initiated the AAAA lookup; pull any preceding failed Graph/login.microsoftonline.com auth on the same host. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, sinkhole/block *.cloudlanecdn.com at DNS and egress, and treat the associated M365 mailbox/app registration as compromised — revoke the service-principal client secret. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all DNS logs for other hosts querying cloudlanecdn.com or its ns1-4 nameservers, and look for logAzure.txt drops and AzureCommunication.dll/uxtheme.dll on those hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "cloudlanecdn.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Defender does not expose DNS query-type; any resolution/connection to cloudlanecdn.com is the C2 domain
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where QueryTypeName == "AAAA"
| where Name endswith "cloudlanecdn.com"
| extend ConfigRecovery = iff(Name matches regex @"\.(p|q)\.cloudlanecdn\.com$", "yes", "no")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryTypeName, ResultCodeName, ConfigRecovery
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CAV3RN AzureCommunication.dll config file 'logAzure.txt' written to disk AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the module's on-disk configuration cache logAzure.txt, which AzureCommunication.dll writes (serialized JSON containing TenantId, ClientId, ClientSecret, target mailbox, DNS bootstrap host and RSA keys) when no prior config file exists. The filename is hardcoded and resolved against the host process working directory, making it a high-fidelity single-string artifact. Rationale: logAzure.txt is a hardcoded, unique filename from the article that stores the module's live Graph credentials and RSA keys — its creation is a near-zero-FP install/staging artifact. Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/ • https://securelist.com/project-cav3rn-cyberespionage-framework-using-outlook-and-dns/120757/
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated bespoke application coincidentally naming an Azure log file logAzure.txt (rare — most Azure SDK logs use different names)
  • Developer/test tooling on an engineer workstation writing a similarly named debug log
  • Backup/restore operations replaying a captured filesystem containing the artifact
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Program Files\\Microsoft"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the folder path and the initiating process — the working directory reveals the host process loading the DLL; capture that process and any sibling DLLs. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host and preserve logAzure.txt for forensics (it exposes the compromised tenant/mailbox and app client secret), then revoke the exposed service-principal secret and rotate the mailbox credentials. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the initiating process hash across the fleet, hunt for AzureCommunication.dll/uxtheme.dll/n-HTCommp.dll and cloudlanecdn.com DNS.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "logAzure.txt"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "logAzure.txt"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CAV3RN framework module DLLs loaded/dropped (AzureCommunication / n-HTCommp / masqueraded uxtheme) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the CAV3RN Native-AOT components by distinctive filename, known MD5, and by uxtheme.dll masquerading (a legitimate System32 DLL name loaded from a non-system path). Catches both the current AzureCommunication.dll communication module and the prior n-HTCommp.dll, plus the uxtheme.dll controller. Rationale: Uses the exact module filenames (AzureCommunication.dll, n-HTCommp.dll) and the three article MD5s, plus the uxtheme.dll masquerade heuristic (legit name off the system path) — all directly named in the article and corroborated by Check Point/Group-IB as CAV3RN/Cavern components. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/cavern-manticore-exposing-iran-linked-modular-c2-framework/ • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1574.001 T1027.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A third-party product legitimately shipping a file named AzureCommunication.dll (uncommon — no known benign product uses this name)
  • uxtheme.dll present in a legitimate application-local WinSxS-style redirection folder not covered by the path exclusions
  • Software installers temporarily extracting a uxtheme.dll to a temp path during patching
  • Antivirus quarantine/restore replaying the sample hash
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the load path and initiating (host) process; a non-system uxtheme.dll or an AzureCommunication.dll under a user-writable path is high confidence. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block the MD5s at EDR, and quarantine the DLLs; treat the tenant/mailbox in any co-resident logAzure.txt as compromised. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot the host process and hashes fleet-wide, then correlate with cloudlanecdn.com DNS and graph.microsoft.com egress from the same hosts.

    or (FileName =~ "uxtheme.dll" and FolderPath !has "\\System32\\" and FolderPath !has "\\SysWOW64\\" and FolderPath !has "\\WinSxS\\")
    or (MD5 in~ ("caf021dda726b8ba049c2aa395e505a1","c092b02fbc0fdf7ee9608dd016673806","29b2b8c5d99f05bfcdd0d8d976eb5678"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

ImFileEvent

    or (TargetFileName =~ "uxtheme.dll" and TargetFilePath !has "\\System32\\" and TargetFilePath !has "\\SysWOW64\\" and TargetFilePath !has "\\WinSxS\\")
    or (TargetFileMD5 in~ ("caf021dda726b8ba049c2aa395e505a1","c092b02fbc0fdf7ee9608dd016673806","29b2b8c5d99f05bfcdd0d8d976eb5678"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileMD5, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Anomalous DLL-host process reaching Microsoft Graph/login.microsoftonline for calendar C2 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Outlook-calendar dead-drop C2: a DLL-host process (rundll32/regsvr32/dllhost) — not a browser or Office app — authenticating to login.microsoftonline.com and calling graph.microsoft.com, which is how AzureCommunication.dll acquires an app token and reads/writes calendar events. Pairs the unusual process with legitimate-but-abused Microsoft cloud endpoints. Rationale: Ties the article's Graph OAuth client_credentials flow (login.microsoftonline.com/.../oauth2/v2.0/token) and graph.microsoft.com organization/calendar calls to an atypical DLL-host process, since AzureCommunication.dll is a Native-AOT DLL executed via a controller rather than a browser/Office client; kept hunting-tier because the cloud endpoints are legitimately used. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-hollowgraph-malware-uses-microsoft-graph-for-stealthy-c2-comms/ • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001 T1550.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • rundll32/dllhost hosting a legitimate Office/OneDrive/Teams COM component that brokers a Graph call
  • Enterprise device-management or licensing agents invoking Graph via a scripted rundll32 wrapper
  • IT automation scripts using regsvr32/rundll32 shims that touch login.microsoftonline.com for token acquisition
  • A signed line-of-business add-in running from AppData that legitimately uses Microsoft Graph
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("OneDrive","Teams","Office"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the initiating process command line and loaded modules — look for a Native-AOT DLL exporting QueryInterface or a co-resident logAzure.txt / cloudlanecdn.com resolution on the same host. Step 2 (contain): If confirmed, isolate the host, revoke the app registration's client secret and the mailbox tokens, and block egress for that process. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate calendar events dated 2050 (subject prefix 'Event ID:' / suffix '1500') in the implicated mailbox via Graph/eDiscovery, and sweep other hosts for the same DLL-host→Graph pattern.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("graph.microsoft.com","login.microsoftonline.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","dllhost.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\AppData\\","\\Temp\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Public\\")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Endpoints=make_set(RemoteUrl), Count=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where array_length(Endpoints) >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("graph.microsoft.com","login.microsoftonline.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","dllhost.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Endpoints=make_set(RemoteUrl), Count=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| eval delta = _time - prev_time
