    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Clop CVE-2025-61882 Oracle EBS exploitation via BI Publisher TemplatePreview / SyncServlet URIs AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the specific Oracle E-Business Suite endpoints abused in the CVE-2025-61882 unauthenticated RCE chain (SyncServlet auth-bypass, configurator/UiServlet return_url SSRF, and the TemplatePreviewPG BI Publisher template-preview). This is the exact initial-access step behind the Estée Lauder / Clop HR-data breach and the wider mass-exploitation campaign. Rationale: Uses the exact URI paths (/OA_HTML/SyncServlet, /OA_HTML/configurator/UiServlet, /OA_HTML/RF.jsp, TemplatePreviewPG) documented by CrowdStrike, Mandiant and WatchTowr as the CVE-2025-61882 exploit chain; these strings do not appear in normal EBS user traffic, giving very high fidelity for the article's initial-access vector. Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/crowdstrike-identifies-campaign-targeting-oracle-e-business-suite-zero-day-CVE-2025-61882/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/oracle-ebusiness-suite-zero-day-exploitation • https://www.oligo.security/blog/cve-2025-61882-oracle-e-business-suite-zero-day-exploited-in-clop-extortion-campaigns
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator previewing a BI Publisher / XML Publisher template via TemplatePreviewPG during report development
  • Oracle-supported patch validation or health-check scripts hitting SyncServlet after CPU application
  • Authorized penetration test or vulnerability scan (e.g. Qualys/Tenable) probing the same CVE-2025-61882 endpoints
  • Internal monitoring/synthetic transaction tooling polling /OA_HTML/ URLs for uptime
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8") // scope to external/untrusted sources; drop known internal admin jump hosts and authorized scanner IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull full request/response for the matching URI, note source IP and whether it is internal admin vs external; check scStatus/EventOutcome — a 200 on TemplatePreviewPG or SyncServlet from an untrusted IP is a likely successful exploit. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/perimeter, isolate the EBS app-tier host, and rotate EBS APPS/application credentials; confirm the Oct-2025 CVE-2025-61882 patch is applied (EBS 12.2.3–12.2.14). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'Oracle EBS Java service spawning shell' and the Clop C2 beacon UC on the same host, and inspect XDO_TEMPLATES_B for rogue TemplateCode values beginning TMP/DEF.
let ebsUris = dynamic(["/OA_HTML/SyncServlet","/OA_HTML/configurator/UiServlet","/OA_HTML/RF.jsp"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where (csUriStem has_any (ebsUris)) or (csUriQuery has "TemplatePreviewPG")
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIP=cIP, Method=csMethod, Uri=csUriStem, Query=csUriQuery, Status=scStatus, UserAgent=csUserAgent),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where (RequestURL has_any (ebsUris)) or (RequestURL has "TemplatePreviewPG")
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=DestinationHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, Method=RequestMethod, Uri=RequestURL, Status=tostring(EventOutcome), UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Oracle EBS Java app-tier service spawning shell / reverse shell (CVE-2025-61882 post-exploitation) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Oracle E-Business Suite Java process (Concurrent Processing / BI Publisher app tier) spawning a Unix shell, scripting interpreter, or reverse-shell command line — the RCE outcome of CVE-2025-61882. Anchors on the article campaign's confirmed reverse-shell (/bin/bash -i >& /dev/tcp) and dropped exploit scripts (exp.py, server.py, oracle_ebs_nday_exploit*.zip). Rationale: Parent=java (the EBS Concurrent Processing/BI Publisher tier) spawning bash/python with the campaign's exact reverse-shell string (/bin/bash -i >& /dev/tcp) and dropped tooling (exp.py, server.py, oracle_ebs_nday_exploit*.zip) is the confirmed CVE-2025-61882 RCE outcome; the parent+child+cmdline combination makes it near-zero-FP on a production EBS host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/crowdstrike-identifies-campaign-targeting-oracle-e-business-suite-zero-day-CVE-2025-61882/ • https://www.oligo.security/blog/cve-2025-61882-oracle-e-business-suite-zero-day-exploited-in-clop-extortion-campaigns
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Oracle EBS custom concurrent programs that legitimately shell out to host scripts (host-type executables) during batch runs
  • DBA/admin running curl or wget from a shell that was itself launched by a Java-based management console
  • Backup or monitoring agents invoking python/perl helpers under the applmgr account
  • Approved patch/clone (adop/rapidclone) automation that spawns shells from Java utilities
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("adop","rapidclone","$APPL_TOP") and AccountName =~ "applmgr") // suppress known EBS patch/clone host-script automation while keeping reverse-shell strings
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child command line and destination (IP:port in the /dev/tcp string); confirm the parent java is the EBS app-tier (applmgr context) and whether the child made outbound connections. 2) Contain: kill the child process, isolate the host from the network, and block the reverse-shell destination IP at the firewall; snapshot for forensics before reboot. 3) Hunt: correlate with the CVE-2025-61882 exploit-URI UC on the same host, search for exp.py/server.py/oracle_ebs_nday_exploit*.zip on disk, and check for the Clop C2 IPs and SAGE*/GOLDVEIN Java implants for persistence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "java" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("oracle.apps","XMLPublisher","XDOTemplate","FNDLIBR")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","ksh","python","python3","perl","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp","bash -i","exp.py","server.py","oracle_ebs_nday_exploit")
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"-i\s*>&\s*/dev/tcp"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "java" or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("oracle.apps","XMLPublisher","FNDLIBR")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","ksh","python","perl","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp","bash -i","exp.py","server.py","oracle_ebs_nday_exploit")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Clop CVE-2025-61882 Oracle EBS C2 / exfiltration beacon to known infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections and DNS resolutions to the confirmed Clop command-and-control and data-exfiltration infrastructure tied to the CVE-2025-61882 Oracle EBS campaign that breached Estée Lauder. Matches the campaign's hardcoded C2 IPs and the pubstorm.com/pubstorm.net (and oa.88tech.me) domains. Rationale: The five C2 IPs are cross-confirmed by CrowdStrike, Mandiant, Oligo and BleepingComputer as CVE-2025-61882 Clop infrastructure, and pubstorm.com/.net were pre-extracted from the article; any host contacting them — especially the EBS app tier — is a strong compromise/exfiltration signal for exactly the breach described. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/oracle-patches-ebs-zero-day-exploited-in-clop-data-theft-attacks/ • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/crowdstrike-identifies-campaign-targeting-oracle-e-business-suite-zero-day-CVE-2025-61882/ • https://www.oligo.security/blog/cve-2025-61882-oracle-e-business-suite-zero-day-exploited-in-clop-extortion-campaigns
ATT&CKT1071 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or sandbox/detonation appliance deliberately connecting to the IOCs for validation
  • Security researcher or IR analyst workstation reproducing the IOC list
  • IP re-assignment after takedown — the address later hosting a benign service (validate against last-seen dates)
  • Passive DNS / TI enrichment tooling resolving pubstorm domains without an actual connection
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MonitoringHost.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("ti-sandbox","malware-detonation")) // exclude security tooling that intentionally touches IOCs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and the initiating process; if the source is the Oracle EBS app-tier host or the process is java/bash, treat as confirmed campaign activity, not a scanner. 2) Contain: block all five C2 IPs and the pubstorm.com/.net + oa.88tech.me domains at firewall/DNS sinkhole, isolate the calling host, and preserve netflow for exfil volume assessment. 3) Hunt: pivot to the CVE-2025-61882 exploit-URI and Java-spawns-shell UCs on the same host, quantify outbound bytes to gauge HR-data exfiltration, and sweep the estate for the SHA256 76b6d36e... and MD5 b296d3b3.../23094d64.../e278700f... payloads.

let c2domains = dynamic(["pubstorm.com","pubstorm.net","oa.88tech.me"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (c2ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (c2domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-61882")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-61882")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |

            - '\svchost.exe'

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("76b6d36e04e367a2334c445b51e1ecce97e4c614e88dfb4f72b104ca0f31235d", "b296d3b3115762096286f225696a9bb1", "23094d64721a279c0ce637584b87d6f1", "e278700f827590c1dff9e24116bde4da") or SHA1 in~ ("76b6d36e04e367a2334c445b51e1ecce97e4c614e88dfb4f72b104ca0f31235d", "b296d3b3115762096286f225696a9bb1", "23094d64721a279c0ce637584b87d6f1", "e278700f827590c1dff9e24116bde4da") or MD5 in~ ("76b6d36e04e367a2334c445b51e1ecce97e4c614e88dfb4f72b104ca0f31235d", "b296d3b3115762096286f225696a9bb1", "23094d64721a279c0ce637584b87d6f1", "e278700f827590c1dff9e24116bde4da")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("76b6d36e04e367a2334c445b51e1ecce97e4c614e88dfb4f72b104ca0f31235d", "b296d3b3115762096286f225696a9bb1", "23094d64721a279c0ce637584b87d6f1", "e278700f827590c1dff9e24116bde4da") or SHA1 in~ ("76b6d36e04e367a2334c445b51e1ecce97e4c614e88dfb4f72b104ca0f31235d", "b296d3b3115762096286f225696a9bb1", "23094d64721a279c0ce637584b87d6f1", "e278700f827590c1dff9e24116bde4da") or MD5 in~ ("76b6d36e04e367a2334c445b51e1ecce97e4c614e88dfb4f72b104ca0f31235d", "b296d3b3115762096286f225696a9bb1", "23094d64721a279c0ce637584b87d6f1", "e278700f827590c1dff9e24116bde4da")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["76b6d36e04e367a2334c445b51e1ecce97e4c614e88dfb4f72b104ca0f31235d", "b296d3b3115762096286f225696a9bb1", "23094d64721a279c0ce637584b87d6f1", "e278700f827590c1dff9e24116bde4da"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SonicWall SMA1000 /wsproxy SSRF to SSH tunnel (CVE-2026-15409) · [LLM] SonicWall SMA1000 command injection via sysCtrl.execRemoveHotfix (CVE-2026-15410) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — SonicWall SMA1000 flaws exploited as zero-days to push custom malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Suo5 reverse-proxy fixed user-agent (UTA0533 SMA implant) · [LLM] ORANGETAIL/Suo5 webshell access via nginx-rewritten SMA routes · [LLM] UTA0533 SonicWall SMA C2 infrastructure network communication · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SonicWall SMA1000 /wsproxy SSRF to SSH tunnel (CVE-2026-15409) AIExploitation High
Hunts UTA0533's pre-auth exploitation of the SMA1000 /wsproxy WebSocket-proxy endpoint to reach internal-only services (SSH/CouchDB/mgmt) via SSRF. Anchors on the exact abuse signature Volexity extracted from extraweb_access.log: /wsproxy requests carrying serviceType=SSH and a negative bmID that complete with an HTTP 101 protocol-switch. Rationale: Uses the exact SSRF signature Volexity pulled from /var/log/aventail/extraweb_access.log ( /wsproxy?bmID=-3389... serviceType=SSH, status 101 ). The 101 Switching-Protocols on an SSH serviceType is the tell that an unauthenticated WebSocket tunnel to an internal-only service succeeded. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://www.securityweek.com/sonicwall-zero-days-exploited-to-deliver-custom-malware-for-weeks-before-patch/
ATT&CKT1190 T1090
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SMA workplace clients that internally use /wsproxy for sanctioned service types (RDP/HTTPS) — filtered here by requiring serviceType=SSH
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) probing /wsproxy post-disclosure
  • SonicWall support/diagnostic tooling replaying WebSocket sessions
  • Internal red-team validation of the CVE after patching
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has "serviceType=RDP" or SyslogMessage has "serviceType=HTTPS")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the appliance firmware is below 12.4.3-03453 / 12.5.0-02835; pull the full extraweb_access.log around the hit and check the source IP against the 8 UTA0533 IPs. 2) Contain: isolate the SMA1000 from the internet, force-expire all VPN sessions, and rotate the appliance product_uuid-derived secrets and admin/CouchDB (admin:admin) credentials. 3) Hunt: on the appliance check /tmp for agent_wp8.jar/agent_wp9.jar/1234.sh, inspect /var/lib/unit/conf.json for rogue routes, and run `find / -perm -4000` for the ROOTRUN/xzfind setuid binary.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where SyslogMessage has "/wsproxy"
| where SyslogMessage has "serviceType=SSH" or SyslogMessage has "bmID=-3389"
| where SyslogMessage has "101"    // WebSocket 'Switching Protocols' == SSRF tunnel established
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SonicWall SMA1000 command injection via sysCtrl.execRemoveHotfix (CVE-2026-15410) AIExploitation High
Hunts the second stage of the UTA0533 chain: root command execution through the Appliance Management Console RPC method sysCtrl.execRemoveHotfix. Anchors on the RPC method name and the path-traversal ('../') hotfix-removal pattern Volexity found in ctrl-service.log. Rationale: sysCtrl.execRemoveHotfix is the specific RPC method Volexity named for the CVE-2026-15410 command injection; combining it with the 'running hotfix removal' + '../' traversal string from ctrl-service.log makes this appliance-specific rather than a generic command-injection template. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/sonicwall-sma-zero-days-exploited.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine administrator removing a hotfix through the AMC as part of patch rollback
  • SonicWall automated update tooling invoking hotfix lifecycle operations
  • Post-incident forensic replay of the RPC by responders
  • Vendor support session performing legitimate hotfix maintenance
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the execRemoveHotfix event time with any authenticated AMC session — legitimate removals come from a logged-in admin, the exploit does not; check for a preceding /wsproxy SSRF hit from the same source IP. 2) Contain: take the appliance offline, snapshot disk+memory for Volexity-style analysis, and block the 8 UTA0533 IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: look for root-context child processes/scripts (deploy_new.py, /tmp/1234.sh) spawned right after the RPC and verify /var/lib/unit/conf.json integrity.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where SyslogMessage has "execRemoveHotfix"
   or (SyslogMessage has "running hotfix removal" and SyslogMessage has "..")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Suo5 reverse-proxy fixed user-agent (UTA0533 SMA implant) AICommand & Control High
Org-wide hunt for the hardcoded, non-existent-browser user-agent the Suo5 (agent_wp8.jar) HTTP forwarding proxy sends when tunnelling through the compromised SMA1000. Because 'Mozilla/6.0 ... AppleWebKit/1537.136' is a fabricated version string, any web/proxy/firewall log carrying it is high-fidelity. Rationale: Volexity states Suo5 requires the specific user-agent 'Mozilla/6.0 (Windows NT 11.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/1537.136'. Mozilla/6.0 and WebKit 1537.136 are non-existent versions, so this string is effectively a unique C2 signature usable across every place HTTP user-agents are logged. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://securityonline.info/sonicwall-sma-zero-day/
ATT&CKT1090 T1572
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners or researchers replaying captured Suo5 traffic in a lab
  • Threat-intel feed validation tools that emit known-bad user-agents on purpose
  • Broken/legacy user-agent spoofing from an obscure legitimate client (rare given the fabricated version)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source and destination of the flagged sessions — the SMA1000 appliance IP appearing as either endpoint confirms active Suo5 tunnelling. 2) Contain: sever the appliance's network path, drop the 8 UTA0533 IPs, and terminate the CommandStartup Java process hosting the injected JAR. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same src/dst pair for the ORANGETAIL webshell routes (/__api__/login, /__api__/logout, error.jsp) and enumerate internal hosts the proxy reached for lateral-movement scope.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RequestClientApplication has "Mozilla/6.0" and RequestClientApplication has "AppleWebKit/1537.136"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ORANGETAIL/Suo5 webshell access via nginx-rewritten SMA routes AICommand & Control High
Hunts interaction with the UTA0533 implants exposed by the attacker's nginx rewrite of /var/lib/unit/conf.json. Anchors on POST requests to the ORANGETAIL webshell routes (/__api__/login, /__api__/logout) and to the abused error pages /workplace/error.jsp and /workplace/dialogs/errorDialog.jsp — endpoints that legitimately only serve GET error content. Rationale: Volexity documents the attacker rewriting nginx (/var/lib/unit/conf.json) to expose /__api__/login and /__api__/logout to the ORANGETAIL webshell, plus Suo5/ORANGETAIL served from /workplace/error.jsp and errorDialog.jsp. A POST to a JSP error page or these API auth routes is inherently anomalous, making the method+path combination high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195626/hacking/volexity-uncovers-zero-day-campaign-targeting-sonicwall-vpn-appliances.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SMA login/logout flow if a future firmware genuinely serves POST /__api__/login (verify against baseline before/after patch)
  • Automated health-check monitors POSTing to appliance API routes
  • Load-balancer probes hitting error.jsp with non-GET methods
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the request came from an external/UTA0533 IP and returned 200 with an unusually large response body (webshell output); a POST to error.jsp is never legitimate. 2) Contain: isolate the appliance, capture /var/lib/unit/conf.json, and remove the rogue nginx routes; kill the CommandStartup process hosting agent_wp8/wp9.jar. 3) Hunt: extract the AES-128-ECB 'find' POST parameter bodies for executed commands, and review internal systems the webshell reached for follow-on activity.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where SyslogMessage has "POST"
| where SyslogMessage has "/__api__/login" or SyslogMessage has "/__api__/logout"
     or SyslogMessage has "/workplace/error.jsp" or SyslogMessage has "/workplace/dialogs/errorDialog.jsp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UTA0533 SonicWall SMA C2 infrastructure network communication AICommand & Control Medium
Retro-hunt and alert for connections to the eight UTA0533 non-VPN C2 IPs Volexity attributed to the SMA1000 campaign. Covers both the appliance beaconing out and any internal host reached/pivoted through the compromised device. Corroborated IOCs shipped by Volexity's primary report. Rationale: The eight IPs are Volexity's attributed non-VPN infrastructure for UTA0533. As explicit atomic IOCs cross-checked against the primary report, any connection to/from them is high-fidelity; querying both src and dst catches both appliance egress and inbound operator access. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://www.securityweek.com/sonicwall-zero-days-exploited-to-deliver-custom-malware-for-weeks-before-patch/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IP reassignment/rotation — hosting-provider IPs (Volexity notes bulletproof/VPS use) may later serve benign tenants, causing stale-IOC hits
  • Threat-intel platform or sandbox detonating the sample and beaconing to these IPs
  • Security team actively probing the C2 for validation
  • Shared NAT egress making attribution to a single host ambiguous
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal endpoint or appliance on the other end of the flow and the process (InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName) driving it; prioritise if the peer is the SMA1000. 2) Contain: block all eight IPs at the perimeter, isolate the involved host/appliance, and preserve netflow + memory. 3) Hunt: sweep for the campaign's file IOCs (deploy_new.py SHA256 8c470301..., agent_wp8.jar 1e1e68bb..., agent_wp9.jar ea9154e3..., xzfind 81a9af38...) and check DNS/proxy logs for repeat beaconing patterns to the same ASNs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("108.205.8.173","147.45.51.19","150.241.210.53","202.8.105.201","217.77.15.99","42.200.172.14","81.19.140.217","89.117.20.1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2 = dynamic(["108.205.8.173","147.45.51.19","150.241.210.53","202.8.105.201","217.77.15.99","42.200.172.14","81.19.140.217","89.117.20.1"]);
CommonSecurityLog

| where DestinationIP in (c2) or SourceIP in (c2)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, Activity
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-15409", "CVE-2026-15410")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-15409", "CVE-2026-15410")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Vulnerable node-tar (<=7.5.18) present on hosts — CVE-2026-59873 decompression-bomb DoS exposure AIWeaponization High
Surfaces every host where Defender/vuln-scanner telemetry reports the npm 'tar' package at or below 7.5.18, the range vulnerable to CVE-2026-59873 (unbounded decompressed-data DoS / Gzip bomb). This is the attack-surface inventory pivot: any service extracting untrusted archives with this version can be forced to exhaust disk/CPU with a tiny crafted input. Fixed in 7.5.19. Rationale: Pivots on the exact CVE id and the concrete affected range from the advisory (npm 'tar' <= 7.5.18, fixed 7.5.19). CVE-id equality in TVM/scanner data is a high-fidelity exposure list with near-zero FP — the only 'noise' is remediated-but-not-rescanned hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-59874 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-23hp-3jrh-7fpw • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-59874 • https://github.com/isaacs/node-tar/security

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host patched to 7.5.19+ but not yet re-scanned, so TVM snapshot is stale
  • 'tar' package pinned inside a container image layer that never extracts untrusted input (internal build tarballs only)
  • Nested/transitive copy of tar in node_modules of a dev-only dependency not reachable at runtime
  • Scanner fingerprints a vendored copy of tar sources without a functioning install
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the flagged host actually runs a service that extracts attacker-supplied archives (npm registry mirror, CI/CD artifact unpack, file-upload/import feature) — internal-only tarball handling is lower priority. 2) Contain: schedule `npm i tar@7.5.19` (or bump the transitive pin via overrides/resolutions) on internet-facing extractors first; add a temporary reverse-proxy body-size cap on upload endpoints. 3) Hunt: pull last 7d of file-write telemetry for the host's node processes and run UC2 to check whether a decompression bomb was already attempted.

node.js process rapidly writing multi-GB file during archive extraction (CVE-2026-59873 gzip-bomb impact) AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts the runtime signature of the node-tar decompression bomb: a node process extracting an archive and writing an abnormally large single file (multi-GB) from a tiny compressed input, driving toward disk exhaustion. Article-specific because the vuln has no total-bytes/entry-count guard, so extraction writes far more data than the input warrants. Rationale: Targets the article's core impact — node-tar writes gigabytes to disk from a negligible compressed stream because there is no cumulative-bytes limit. Pivots on node as the initiating process plus an anomalous single-file size / write-volume, the observable footprint of the Gzip bomb described in the PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-23hp-3jrh-7fpw • https://github.com/isaacs/node-tar/security
ATT&CKT1499.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate large-artifact extraction in CI (multi-GB container layers, ML model tarballs, dataset archives)
  • Node-based backup/restore or migration jobs that genuinely unpack large archives
  • Log-rotation or cache builds where a node service writes a large single file
  • Package-mirror sync (e.g. Verdaccio/nexus) unpacking large legitimate packages
  • Electron/build tooling emitting a large bundled asset
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("backup","restore","webpack","electron-builder","model","dataset") or FolderPath has_any ("\\ci\\","\\build\\","\\artifacts\\","/ci/","/build/","/artifacts/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and FolderPath — is this a known CI/build/backup job writing to an expected artifact path, or an internet-facing upload/import service writing to a temp/extraction dir? Correlate the host against UC1 (is tar<=7.5.18 present?). 2) Contain: if unexplained, kill the node PID and quarantine the source archive; add disk-quota/ulimit on the extraction directory and a body-size limit on the upload endpoint. 3) Hunt: search the same host+window for the inbound tiny archive (small POST/upload immediately preceding the write burst) and for repeated attempts across other extractor hosts.

LightRAG destructive document ops post-bypass (DELETE /documents, clear_cache, unauth upload) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the impact stage of CVE-2026-61740 exploitation: destructive or ingestion calls to the LightRAG document API — DELETE /documents (wipes the corpus), /documents/clear_cache (destroys LLM/embedding caches) and /documents/upload|scan|file_batch (attacker-controlled ingestion). These are inherently rare, high-consequence operations that map directly to the advisory's confidentiality/integrity/availability impact. Rationale: Uses the exact destructive LightRAG endpoints named in the advisory impact section — DELETE /documents, /documents/clear_cache, /documents/upload|scan|file_batch|texts — which are rare, high-consequence operations. The DELETE-against-/documents shape is the corpus-wipe primitive the PoC demonstrated returning HTTP 200. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f4vv-55c2-5789 • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-61740
ATT&CKT1485 T1496 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Administrator performing a legitimate corpus refresh (bulk /documents/upload or /documents/scan) during scheduled re-ingestion
  • Operational runbook clearing caches via /documents/clear_cache after a model/embedding change
  • A data pipeline that deletes and reloads the knowledge base on a schedule (DELETE /documents followed by re-upload)
  • CI / staging environments exercising the document API during automated tests
  • Backup/migration tooling snapshotting then clearing the document store
Suppression filter
| where RequestMethod =~ "DELETE"   // narrow to the pure corpus-destruction primitive, dropping benign upload/scan/cache-clear ingestion noise
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the SourceIP and RequestMethod/RequestURL; confirm whether the call carried an X-API-Key (legitimate ops) or was preceded by a Bearer guest-JWT request (UC1) from the same IP — the latter confirms CVE-2026-61740 abuse. Check whether a change window/runbook explains it. 2) CONTAIN: Block the SourceIP, take the LightRAG instance off the public interface, and upgrade to lightrag-hku >=1.5.4; rotate TOKEN_SECRET and LIGHTRAG_API_KEY. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every document/graph/query call from that IP to quantify what was read, deleted, ingested (potential poisoning) or queried (LLM-credit exhaustion), and diff the current document store against the last backup to assess destruction.

LightRAG CVE-2026-61736: cross-origin credentialed read of /documents or /query (data exfil) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts credentialed cross-origin HTTP requests to LightRAG's sensitive API endpoints (/documents, /query, /query/data) where the Referer/Origin host differs from the LightRAG host — the exploitation signature of the CORS wildcard + allow_credentials flaw. A malicious site the victim visits rides their authenticated session to exfiltrate documents and knowledge-graph data. Rationale: Anchored on LightRAG's article-named endpoints (/login, /documents) plus /query corroborated by the official API docs, combined with the CORS root cause: the exploit necessarily produces a credentialed request whose Referer/Origin host != the LightRAG host. Comparing referer-host to target-host is the highest-fidelity behavioural signal the flaw leaves in access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.thehackerwire.com/lightrag-critical-credentialed-cors-vulnerability/ • https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG/blob/main/docs/LightRAG-API-Server.md • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-61736
ATT&CKT1185 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Split frontend/backend deployment where the LightRAG SPA is served from a different host/subdomain than the API, so legitimate reads carry a cross-origin Referer
  • API gateway or reverse proxy that rewrites Host, making Referer host legitimately differ from the logged CsHost
  • Grafana/BI dashboards or internal wikis embedding LightRAG query results with their own Referer
  • Swagger UI / ReDoc API console hosted on a separate documentation host
  • DAST scanners (Burp, OWASP ZAP) issuing requests with crafted Referer values
Suppression filter
| extend RefDomain = strcat_array(array_slice(split(RefererHost,"."), -2, -1), ".") | extend TgtDomain = strcat_array(array_slice(split(TargetHost,"."), -2, -1), ".") | where RefDomain != TgtDomain
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending RefererHost and CIp; confirm it is NOT a sanctioned internal frontend/gateway for this LightRAG instance and check whether the CsUsername session was concurrently active from a normal client. 2) Contain: set CORS_ORIGINS to an explicit allow-list (or allow_credentials=False) and upgrade lightrag-hku to >=1.5.4; if the RefererHost is an unknown external domain, block it at the proxy/WAF and force-invalidate active LightRAG tokens. 3) Hunt: sweep all LightRAG access logs for the same RefererHost across /documents, /query, /query/data and DELETE /documents; review volume of documents/knowledge-graph rows read to scope data exposure.

| where CsUriStem has_any ("/documents", "/query")
| where CsMethod in ("GET","POST")
| where isnotempty(Referer) and Referer != "-"
| extend RefererHost = tolower(tostring(parse_url(Referer).Host))
| extend TargetHost = tolower(tostring(split(CsHost, ":")[0]))
| where isnotempty(RefererHost) and RefererHost != TargetHost
| where RefererHost !in ("localhost", "127.0.0.1")
| project TimeGenerated, CsHost, CIp, CsUsername, CsMethod, CsUriStem, Referer, RefererHost, UserAgent, ScStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LightRAG CVE-2026-61736: cross-origin DELETE of document store (destructive CORS abuse) AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on a credentialed cross-origin DELETE against LightRAG's /documents endpoints where the Referer/Origin host differs from the LightRAG host. The advisory calls out 'deleting the entire document store' as a destructive impact of the wildcard-CORS-with-credentials flaw; a DELETE riding the victim's session from an external origin is high-fidelity data destruction. Rationale: Uses the article's explicitly stated destructive impact (delete the document store) mapped to LightRAG's real DELETE /documents and DELETE /documents/delete_document endpoints (confirmed in the API-server docs), qualified by the cross-origin Referer signature that only the CORS flaw produces — a very low-FP, high-severity combination. Cross-checked against: • https://www.thehackerwire.com/lightrag-critical-credentialed-cors-vulnerability/ • https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG/blob/main/docs/LightRAG-API-Server.md • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-61736
ATT&CKT1485 T1185
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin performing bulk document deletion from a dedicated management console hosted on a different host than the API
  • Scheduled data-retention / cleanup jobs invoked from an orchestration host whose Referer differs from the API host
  • QA/staging teardown scripts that clear the document store between test runs
  • Split frontend deployment where the admin UI legitimately lives on another subdomain
Suppression filter
| extend RefDomain = strcat_array(array_slice(split(RefererHost,"."), -2, -1), ".") | extend TgtDomain = strcat_array(array_slice(split(TargetHost,"."), -2, -1), ".") | where RefDomain != TgtDomain
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the RefererHost, CIp and CsUsername on the DELETE; verify whether an authorized admin intentionally cleared documents from a sanctioned console — if not, treat as active destruction. 2) Contain: immediately restrict CORS_ORIGINS to an explicit allow-list (or disable allow_credentials) and upgrade to lightrag-hku >=1.5.4; revoke/rotate the affected user's LightRAG token and, if data loss occurred, initiate restore of the document/KG store from backup. 3) Hunt: search for the same RefererHost/CIp across GET /documents and /query (pre-deletion reconnaissance/exfil) and for any /login POSTs from the same origin to establish the full session-riding chain.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsMethod == "DELETE"
| where CsUriStem has "/documents"
| where isnotempty(Referer) and Referer != "-"
| extend RefererHost = tolower(tostring(parse_url(Referer).Host))
| extend TargetHost = tolower(tostring(split(CsHost, ":")[0]))
| where isnotempty(RefererHost) and RefererHost != TargetHost
| where RefererHost !in ("localhost", "127.0.0.1")
| project TimeGenerated, CsHost, CIp, CsUsername, CsMethod, CsUriStem, Referer, RefererHost, UserAgent, ScStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hunts the FakeGit SmartLoader install stage where a batch launcher spawns a LuaJIT runtime (luajit.exe / Compiler.exe / renamed ODE3.exe) that loads lua51.dll and executes an obfuscated single-line Lua script passed as a .txt/.log argument from a user-writable path. This is the specific delivery-to-execution pivot of the counterfeit GitHub-repo ZIP, not generic script execution. Rationale: Anchors on the exact SmartLoader ZIP components (luajit.exe/Compiler.exe/ODE3.exe + userdata.txt) confirmed across Trend Micro, Hexastrike and ASEC write-ups; a LuaJIT interpreter running a .txt/.log script from Downloads/Temp/AppData is not a normal software pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/c/ai-assisted-fake-github-repositories.html • https://hexastrike.com/resources/blog/threat-intelligence/cloned-loaded-and-stolen-how-109-fake-github-repositories-delivered-smartloader-and-stealc/ • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/89551/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate game or app bundling LuaJIT that ships a .log config in its own install dir (rare in Downloads/Temp)
  • Developer running luajit.exe against a .txt test script from a project folder under AppData
  • Redistributable installers extracting to %Temp% that legitimately embed lua51.dll
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a lab
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("devenv.exe","steam.exe") and FolderPath has @"\Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree — confirm parent is Launcher.bat/cmd.exe and that lua51.dll loaded from the same user-writable folder; hash the luajit.exe and .txt script and check size (SmartLoader Lua scripts are ~296-309 KB single-line). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the luajit/ODE3 process tree, and block the source GitHub release URL if recoverable from FileOriginUrl. 3) Hunt: search the same host for %AppData%\ODE3 drops and a 'SecurityHealthService_ODE3' scheduled task (UC2) and outbound C2 to pasteflawwed[.]world / Polygon RPC (UC3) to confirm SmartLoader→StealC progression.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("luajit.exe","Compiler.exe","ODE3.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("luajit.exe","Compiler.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("userdata.txt",".txt",".log")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(TargetUserName endswith "$")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("luajit.exe","Compiler.exe","ODE3.exe") or ParentProcessName has_any ("luajit.exe","Compiler.exe","Launcher.bat")
| where CommandLine has_any ("userdata.txt",".txt",".log")
| where CommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 6f3a1c8e-9d21-4b77-8f1a-2c4e5b7a9d10
description: Detects FakeGit/SmartLoader LuaJIT loader chain where luajit.exe or a renamed copy executes an obfuscated .txt/.log Lua script from a user-writable path
references:

logsource:

detection:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\luajit.exe OR *\\Luajit.exe OR *\\LUAJIT.EXE OR *\\Compiler.exe OR *\\compiler.exe OR *\\ODE3.exe OR *\\ode3.exe) @CommandLine:(*userdata.txt* OR *.txt* OR *.log*) @CommandLine:(*\\Downloads\\* OR *\\Temp\\* OR *\\AppData\\* OR *\\Public\\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(luajit|compiler|ode3)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(userdata\.txt|\.txt|\.log)/i
| regex("(?i)\\\\(Downloads|Temp|AppData|Public)\\\\", field=CommandLine)

SmartLoader persistence: LuaJIT runtime copied to %AppData%\ODE3 (module.class/lua51.dll) AIInstallation High
Detects the SmartLoader persistence stage that copies the renamed LuaJIT runtime (ODE3.exe), a module.class blob, and lua51.dll into %AppData%\Roaming\ODE3, later registered as scheduled task 'SecurityHealthService_ODE3'. The module.class filename beside lua51.dll in a per-user Roaming folder is a highly specific FakeGit artifact. Rationale: module.class + lua51.dll + ODE3.exe co-located in %AppData%\ODE3 is the exact persistence artifact documented by intellibron/ASEC; requiring >=2 of the three artifacts in the same folder near-eliminates coincidental hits. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.intellibron.io/lua-jit-smartloader-analyzing-the-github-campaign-delivering-stealer/ • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/89551/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/c/ai-assisted-fake-github-repositories.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated legitimate app that happens to use an 'ODE3' product folder (uncommon)
  • Backup/sync tools (OneDrive, Dropbox) replicating a previously-infected AppData tree — writer will be the sync client, not luajit
  • Analyst restoring quarantined files during IR (writer = AV/EDR)
  • Java-based app writing a real module.class but NOT alongside lua51.dll in an ODE3 folder (the >=2 artifact gate filters this)
Suppression filter
| where Writer !in~ ("onedrive.exe","dropbox.exe","googledrivefs.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) is luajit.exe/Compiler.exe rather than a sync client; enumerate the ODE3 folder contents and check for a 'SecurityHealthService_ODE3' scheduled task (schtasks /query or DeviceEvents ScheduledTaskCreated). 2) Contain: isolate host, delete the scheduled task, remove %AppData%\ODE3, and kill any running ODE3.exe. 3) Hunt: pivot to the loader-chain execution (UC1) to find the originating ZIP and to C2 telemetry (UC3) for pasteflawwed[.]world / Polygon RPC beaconing indicating StealC staging.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has @"\ODE3\"
| where FileName in~ ("ODE3.exe","module.class","lua51.dll")
| summarize Artifacts=make_set(FileName), Writer=any(InitiatingProcessFileName), WriterCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp) by DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where array_length(Artifacts) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\ODE3\"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("ODE3.exe","module.class","lua51.dll")
| summarize Artifacts=make_set(TargetFileName), Writer=any(ActingProcessName), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername
| where array_length(Artifacts) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc

SmartLoader blockchain C2: non-browser process resolving pasteflawwed[.]world / Polygon eth_call dead-drop AICommand & Control High
Detects SmartLoader command-and-control where the LuaJIT runtime (luajit.exe/ODE3.exe/Compiler.exe) beacons to the FakeGit C2 domain pasteflawwed[.]world or issues JSON-RPC eth_call requests to public Polygon RPC endpoints to retrieve the next-stage StealC payload from a smart-contract dead-drop resolver. Rationale: pasteflawwed[.]world is the named SmartLoader C2 domain and the Polygon eth_call dead-drop resolver is the campaign's documented blockchain C2 (Trend Micro/Hexastrike); gating the RPC endpoints on a luajit/ODE3 initiating process avoids flagging legitimate crypto tooling. Cross-checked against: • https://hexastrike.com/resources/blog/threat-intelligence/cloned-loaded-and-stolen-how-109-fake-github-repositories-delivered-smartloader-and-stealc/ • https://www.planetjon.net/news/cybersecurity/smartloader-stealc-campaign-blockchain-c2-and-fraudulent-github-repositories/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/c/ai-assisted-fake-github-repositories.html
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web3/DeFi developer wallet or MetaMask backend resolving Polygon RPC (initiating process is a browser/node, not luajit — excluded by the process gate)
  • Blockchain analytics or node software polling rpc.ankr.com from a server
  • Threat-intel or sandbox appliance resolving pasteflawwed[.]world during analysis
  • DNS sinkhole / security proxy re-resolving the IOC for blocking
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","node.exe","metamask.exe") or RemoteUrl has "pasteflawwed.world"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process behind the DNS/connection — in Defender confirm InitiatingProcessFileName is luajit.exe/ODE3.exe; a LuaJIT runtime issuing eth_call JSON-RPC is not legitimate. 2) Contain: isolate host, block pasteflawwed[.]world and the abused Polygon RPC FQDNs at egress, and kill/quarantine the ODE3 process tree. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the ODE3 persistence folder and scheduled task (UC2) and the original loader execution (UC1); sweep other hosts for the same C2 resolution and check for StealC exfil (credential-store access, browser DB reads) following the beacon.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteUrl has "pasteflawwed.world")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("luajit.exe","ODE3.exe","Compiler.exe")
        and RemoteUrl has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","polygon.llamarpc.com","rpc.ankr.com","polygon.drpc.org"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("pasteflawwed.world","polygon-rpc.com","polygon.llamarpc.com","rpc.ankr.com","polygon.drpc.org")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

    object payload signature.
references:

tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

        ParentImage|endswith:

            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc
