Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] HollowGraph logAzure.txt Entra credential config drop · [LLM] New Entra client secret on Graph-capable OAuth app (HollowGraph access upkeep) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Application-driven M365 calendar writes (HollowGraph Graph dead-drop) · [LLM] HollowGraph DNS credential-refresh channel to cloudlanecdn.com (AAAA) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] HollowGraph far-future 2050 calendar dead-drop signatures (subject GUID / File{n}.txt) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Application-driven M365 calendar writes (HollowGraph Graph dead-drop) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts Microsoft 365 calendar/appointment items that are created or updated by an application or service principal rather than a human, which is how HollowGraph plants tasking and uploads exfil attachments through legitimate Microsoft Graph traffic. Article-specific because it pivots on the app-principal actor performing Exchange calendar CRUD, the exact dead-drop mechanism Group-IB documented. Rationale: Group-IB's core finding is calendar events written by an app rather than a person via Graph; UserType=Application on Exchange Appointment Create/Update is the highest-fidelity behavioural signature that survives the fact that no attacker domain is contacted. Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-hollowgraph-malware-uses-microsoft-graph-for-stealthy-c2-comms/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft Bookings / scheduling apps creating appointment items on shared mailboxes
  • Teams meeting add-ins and room-finder services writing calendar events via app permissions
  • Third-party calendar-sync SaaS (Calendly, Reclaim, Zoom) with delegated Graph Calendars.ReadWrite
  • Backup/eDiscovery tools enumerating and re-writing calendar items
  • Migration tooling (BitTitan/Quest) creating appointments during mailbox moves
Suppression filter
| where not(ClientInfoString has_any ("MicrosoftBooking","SchedulingService","Calendly","Reclaim") or AccountDisplayName has_any ("Bookings","Room Finder","Calendar Sync"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the AppId/ServicePrincipal writing the events; check if it is a sanctioned Bookings/scheduling app and whether the target mailbox normally receives app-driven calendar writes. Inspect ItemAttachments and Subject for File{n}.txt / GUID naming. Step 2 (contain): If unrecognised, revoke the app's Graph consent and disable the service principal, then reset the compromised mailbox credentials and revoke sessions. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate every mailbox this app touched, pull all calendar items it created (esp. far-future dates), and pivot to UC covering 2050-05-13 subjects and logAzure.txt on endpoints.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application in ("Microsoft Exchange Online","Office 365 Exchange Online","Microsoft Graph")
| where ActionType in ("Create","Update")
| where AccountType == "Application"
| where RawEventData has_any ("Appointment","CalendarItem","IPM.Appointment")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, Application, ApplicationId, ActionType, ObjectName, IPAddress, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where Operation in ("Create","Update")
| where ItemType in ("Appointment","CalendarItem","Meeting")
| where UserType in ("Application","ServicePrincipal")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, MailboxOwnerUPN, Operation, ItemType, ClientIP, ClientIPAddress, ClientInfoString, Subject, ItemAttachments
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
index=o365 sourcetype=o365:management:activity Workload=Exchange (Operation=Create OR Operation=Update)
| search UserType IN ("Application","ServicePrincipal") (ItemType="Appointment" OR ItemType="CalendarItem" OR ItemType="Meeting")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(ItemType) as ItemType values(ClientIP) as ClientIP values(ClientInfoString) as ClientInfoString by UserId MailboxOwnerUPN Operation ClientAppId
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
HollowGraph far-future 2050 calendar dead-drop signatures (subject GUID / File{n}.txt) AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on the concrete content fingerprints of HollowGraph's dead-drop: calendar events dated 2050-05-13, subjects that are a bare GUID or match the Boss{..}ID{..} tasking scheme, and attachments named File{n}.txt. These are the exact operator artefacts Group-IB published, making this a very high-confidence, low-noise detection. Rationale: 2050-05-13, the Boss{..}ID{..} / bare-GUID subject scheme and File{n}.txt attachments are verbatim IOCs from Group-IB's report; a year-2050 calendar event carrying a File1.txt attachment has essentially no benign explanation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/ • https://www.securityweek.com/new-hollowgraph-malware-abuses-microsoft-365-calendar-for-cc-communication/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1567
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 'never-expire' placeholder events some scheduling tools set far in the future (rare and won't carry File{n}.txt)
  • QA/test mailboxes seeded with dummy File1.txt attachments
  • A user genuinely creating a 2050 milestone/anniversary reminder (won't have GUID subject + File{n}.txt combo)
  • Data-classification tools appending sequential FileN.txt exports to calendar bodies
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the flagged event; confirm the 2050-05-13 date plus GUID/Boss{}ID{} subject and File{n}.txt attachments co-occur (all three = confirmed HollowGraph). Note the app/actor that wrote it. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the affected mailbox, revoke the writing app's consent and service-principal secrets, force credential reset and session revocation. Preserve the event + attachments as evidence before deletion. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all tenant mailboxes for far-future events and File{n}.txt attachments, and pivot to endpoints for logAzure.txt and DNS to cloudlanecdn.com to find the implant host.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application in ("Microsoft Exchange Online","Office 365 Exchange Online","Microsoft Graph")
| where RawEventData has "2050-05-13"
    or RawEventData matches regex @"(?i)File\d+\.txt"
    or RawEventData matches regex @"(?i)Boss\{.*\}ID\{.*\}"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, AccountType, Application, ActionType, ObjectName, IPAddress, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where (Subject has "2050-05-13")
    or (EventData has "2050-05-13")
    or (ItemAttachments matches regex @"(?i)File\d+\.txt")
    or (Subject matches regex @"(?i)Boss\{.*\}ID\{.*\}")
| project TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, UserId, Operation, ItemType, Subject, ItemAttachments, ClientIP, UserType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
index=o365 sourcetype=o365:management:activity Workload=Exchange
| search ("2050-05-13" OR Subject="*2050-05-13*" OR Subject="*Boss{*}ID{*}*" OR "File1.txt" OR "File2.txt")
| rex field=Item.Attachments "(?<HgAttach>File\d+\.txt)"
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Subject) as Subject values(HgAttach) as HgAttach values(ClientIP) as ClientIP by MailboxOwnerUPN UserId Operation ItemType
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
HollowGraph DNS credential-refresh channel to cloudlanecdn.com (AAAA) AICommand & Control High
Detects the cleartext DNS side-channel HollowGraph uses to refresh its Entra client-credentials, decoding tenant ID/client ID/client secret/mailbox from IPv6 AAAA records returned by cloudlanecdn[.]com. Article-specific because it anchors on the named C2 domain and the AAAA record type the malware abuses. Rationale: cloudlanecdn[.]com is a named IOC and the AAAA record type is the specific decode vector Group-IB describes; the domain has no legitimate business use, so any resolution is actionable, and scoping to AAAA further tightens fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-hollowgraph-malware-uses-microsoft-graph-for-stealthy-c2-comms/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1132.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / sandboxes detonating the sample and resolving the domain during analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliances proactively resolving IOC domains
  • A typo-squat/parked-domain sinkhole resolving the name for research
  • Passive-DNS collectors replaying queries
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-analysis"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the host and the ContextImageFileName/InitiatingProcess making the query; confirm it is not a security scanner. Frequent AAAA queries with long high-entropy subdomains under this domain = confirmed. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block cloudlanecdn.com at DNS/egress, and capture memory/the querying process for the .NET implant DLL. Step 3 (hunt): On the host, search for logAzure.txt and the calendar dead-drop activity; across the fleet, look for other hosts querying the same domain within the 3 Jun–9 Jul active window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "cloudlanecdn.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "cloudlanecdn.com"
| where QueryType == 28 or QueryTypeName =~ "AAAA"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName, ResultCode, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HollowGraph logAzure.txt Entra credential config drop AIInstallation High
Detects creation of logAzure.txt, the file HollowGraph disguises as a routine log to store the tenant ID, client ID, client secret and target mailbox decoded from DNS. A precise, low-noise filename IOC that flags the implant host and its stored client-credentials. Rationale: logAzure.txt is a verbatim IOC and the malware's on-disk client-credential store; an exact-filename match is high fidelity because the name is attacker-chosen and not a standard Windows/Azure log artefact. Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/ • https://gbhackers.com/hollowgraph-malware-turns-microsoft-365-calendar-events/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A homegrown script or admin genuinely naming an Azure diagnostic log 'logAzure.txt'
  • Azure SDK/CLI verbose logging redirected to a similarly named file by an engineer
  • Backup software restoring an old file of that name
  • Security researcher replaying the sample in a lab host
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Azure\", @"\Microsoft SDKs\") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("az.exe","pwsh.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-Verbose")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName/ContextImageFileName) and file path; a non-admin process (esp. a .NET host like a rundll/dotnet loader) writing logAzure.txt is confirmed HollowGraph. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, capture logAzure.txt and the writing binary, then rotate/revoke the Entra client secret and app credentials referenced inside it and revoke the app's Graph consent. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot from the file's parent process to the calendar dead-drop (UC1/UC2) and cloudlanecdn.com DNS (UC3), and sweep the fleet for other logAzure.txt drops.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "logAzure.txt"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "logAzure.txt"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New Entra client secret on Graph-capable OAuth app (HollowGraph access upkeep) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts newly added application/service-principal credentials in Entra ID, the mechanism HollowGraph relies on to keep its client-credentials Graph access alive. Group-IB explicitly recommends alerting on newly created client secrets for apps that can reach Graph; this surfaces credential additions for triage against the campaign. Rationale: Group-IB's identity-side guidance is to alert on newly created client secrets for Graph-capable OAuth apps; the DNS channel exists specifically to refresh those client credentials, so credential-add events are a campaign-relevant pivot even though they need enrichment for the Graph mail/calendar permission set. Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/hollowgraph-microsoft-365/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/hollowgraph-microsoft-calendars/
ATT&CKT1098.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine secret rotation by app owners before expiry
  • CI/CD or IaC pipelines (Terraform/Bicep) programmatically adding app credentials
  • Admins onboarding a new legitimate integration that needs Graph access
  • MSP/automation service principals rotating secrets on schedule
Suppression filter
| where Actor !endswith "$" and ActorApp !in~ ("Terraform","Azure DevOps","GitHub Actions") and Actor !has "svc-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the target app and who added the secret; check whether the app holds Mail/Calendars Graph permissions and whether the add correlates with any anomalous sign-in or the campaign window (3 Jun–9 Jul). Step 2 (contain): For unrecognised additions, remove the new credential, disable the service principal, and review the app's granted Graph scopes and recent Graph activity. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate the app's recent mailbox/calendar operations (UC1/UC2), check for the app writing far-future events, and look for logAzure.txt / cloudlanecdn.com on endpoints tied to the actor.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("Add service principal credentials.","Update application \u2013 Certificates and secrets management","Add application credentials")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, ObjectName, ObjectType, IPAddress, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName in ("Add service principal credentials","Update application \u2013 Certificates and secrets management","Add application credentials")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend ActorApp = tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)
| extend TargetApp = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, ActorApp, TargetApp, Result, CorrelationId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

index=azure sourcetype="azure:aad:audit" (operationName="Add service principal credentials" OR operationName="Update application \u2013 Certificates and secrets management" OR operationName="Add application credentials")

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents

Russian Intelligence Hacks IP Cameras to Spy on Military Logistics Across NATO States and Ukraine

The Hacker News
2026-07-20 13 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

At least one Russian intelligence service is systematically hijacking internet-connected security cameras across Europe and Ukraine, using the feeds to watch military transport routes, weapons shipments bound for Kyiv, and the locations of Ukrainian troops. That is the finding of a cybersecurity advisory published July 10 by the AIVD and MIVD, the Netherlands' civilian and military intelligence

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Internet-facing devices carrying the Dropbear/Apache CVEs named in the AIVD IP-camera advisory · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Internet-facing devices carrying the Dropbear/Apache CVEs named in the AIVD IP-camera advisory AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces managed devices flagged internet-facing that carry CVE-2016-7407 (Dropbear dropbearconvert) or CVE-2021-39275 (Apache httpd < 2.4.49) — the two vulnerable services the AIVD/MIVD advisory and Censys highlighted on exposed IP cameras. This is an exposure/attack-surface hunt that operationalises the advisory's top recommendation ('find what is reachable from the public internet'), not a compromise alert. Rationale: Anchored on the only two concrete, article-named strings that survive scrutiny — CVE-2016-7407 (Dropbear dropbearconvert) and CVE-2021-39275 (Apache httpd pre-2.4.49) — pivoted on IsInternetFacing/DeviceCategory to operationalise the advisory's 'find what is exposed' guidance. The pre-extracted IP 212.187.14.204 and domain c14204.upc-c.chello.nl were dropped because no second source (AIVD brochure, The Record, SecurityAffairs) corroborated them. Cross-checked against: • https://english.aivd.nl/documents/2026/07/10/brochure-cybersecurity-advisory-russian-state-actors-are-compromising-ip-cameras • https://therecord.media/russian-intelligence-compromising-cameras-nato-ukraine-netherlands • https://securityaffairs.com/195708/intelligence/dutch-intelligence-warns-russia-uses-hacked-ip-cameras-for-military-espionage.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001 T1133
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Version-banner match where the vulnerable code path isn't reachable — CVE-2021-39275 only bites when a third-party module feeds untrusted data to the affected function (the article's own caveat).
  • CVE-2016-7407 is a local malicious-key-import bug in dropbearconvert, not a remote exploit — an internet-facing hit means exposure/attack surface, not active compromise.
  • Devices flagged IsInternetFacing because of a NAT/public-IP mapping that is actually firewalled at the perimeter.
  • Patched but not yet re-scanned devices still advertising the old service banner.
  • Non-camera hosts (general web servers, NAS, VPN appliances) running the same Apache/Dropbear versions surfacing alongside the cameras you actually care about.
Suppression filter
| where DeviceCategory in~ ("NetworkDevice", "IoT") or DeviceType in~ ("Camera", "IoT", "NetworkDevice") or isnotempty(PublicIP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device is genuinely reachable from the internet (test the port from an external vantage, don't trust the banner alone) and identify whether it is a camera/IoT device overlooking a logistics route, port, loading dock or other sensitive site. 2) Contain: kill the exposure — remove the port-forward/UPnP mapping, place the device behind a VPN, and rotate default/factory credentials; if the device can't support MFA or patching, pull it off the public internet entirely. 3) Hunt: pull the device's own access logs for logins or stream pulls from unrecognised IPs, and run this inventory across the whole estate to enumerate every remaining internet-facing camera so they can be locked down before an operator finds them.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents

| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

| order by files desc

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",

Hugging Face warns an autonomous AI agent hacked its network

BleepingComputer
2026-07-20 7 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Hugging Face artificial intelligence repository disclosed that attackers gained access to internal datasets and credentials after breaching its production infrastructure using an autonomous AI agent system. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1555.003
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Hugging Face malicious-dataset RCE: Python ML worker spawns shell/network tool · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cloud credential theft via IMDS (169.254.169.254) from data-processing worker · [LLM] Cluster/cloud credential harvesting for lateral movement from ML worker · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Hugging Face malicious-dataset RCE: Python ML worker spawns shell/network tool AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the initial code-execution step of the Hugging Face breach, where a malicious dataset abused a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection flaw in the dataset config to run code on a processing worker. Surfaces a Python process running the `datasets`/`load_dataset` pipeline that unexpectedly spawns a shell or network/download binary. Rationale: Anchors on the article's two named code-execution paths (remote-code dataset loader + template injection in dataset config) by pairing a Hugging Face `datasets`/`load_dataset`/`trust_remote_code` parent context with a shell/network child — the observable of RCE on a processing worker. Cross-checked HF's own July-2026 incident post and The Hacker News/Varonis write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://huggingface.co/blog/security-incident-july-2026 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/worlds-largest-ai-model-repository.html • https://www.varonis.com/blog/huggingface-breach
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A dataset-preprocessing script legitimately shelling out to `wget`/`curl` to fetch auxiliary files
  • ML pipeline calling `subprocess`/`os.system` to run `chmod +x` or `base64` on model artifacts
  • Notebook/dev users running `datasets` interactively and spawning a shell for debugging
  • CI jobs that clone a dataset and post-process it with `bash` helper scripts
  • `git-lfs` or conda hooks invoked by a python data job
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("chmod +x","git-lfs","conda") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "ci-runner")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full parent Python command line and the child process args; confirm which dataset/repo was being loaded and whether `trust_remote_code` was set. Inspect the child's downstream network destinations. 2) Contain: isolate the worker/pod, kill the process tree, and block outbound egress from the node; snapshot for forensics before rebuild. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/account for IMDS access (169.254.169.254), reads of ~/.aws/credentials or k8s service-account tokens, and any newly-spawned long-lived listeners or connections to public paste/tunnel services.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("datasets","load_dataset","trust_remote_code","huggingface","hf_datasets")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","scp","chmod","base64")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","python3")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("datasets","load_dataset","trust_remote_code","huggingface","hf_datasets")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","scp","chmod","base64")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hugging Face Malicious Dataset Remote-Code Loader Spawns Shell From Python ML Worker
id: 6f2b9c14-4a1e-4d2c-9b7a-2f1d8e3c9a01
description: Detects a Python process running the Hugging Face datasets pipeline spawning a shell or network/download binary, matching the dataset-loader/template-injection RCE used in the July 2026 Hugging Face breach.
references:
  - https://huggingface.co/blog/security-incident-july-2026
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hugging-face-breach-autonomous-ai-agent-system-internal-datasets-credentials/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/21
tags:
  - attack.t1203
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - 'datasets'
      - 'load_dataset'
      - 'trust_remote_code'
      - 'huggingface'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/scp'
      - '/chmod'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:(*trust_remote_code* OR *load_dataset*) OR (@process.name:(sh OR bash OR dash OR curl OR wget OR nc OR ncat OR scp OR chmod) AND @process.command_line:(*huggingface* OR *datasets* OR *.cache/huggingface*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^python[0-9.]*$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|curl|wget|nc|ncat|scp|chmod|base64)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

Cloud credential theft via IMDS (169.254.169.254) from data-processing worker AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-theft step where the attacker stole cloud credentials after gaining code execution on a Hugging Face processing worker. Flags shell/CLI download tools (not AWS SDKs) reaching the instance metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254 to harvest IAM role credentials. Rationale: Uses the canonical IMDS IP 169.254.169.254 combined with non-SDK tools (curl/wget/shell) — legit boto3/AWS-SDK IMDS access runs inside the SDK, so a shell/download tool hitting the credentials endpoint is high-fidelity for the article's 'stole cloud credentials' step. GuardDuty InstanceCredentialExfiltration provides AWS-native corroboration. Cross-checked against: • https://huggingface.co/blog/security-incident-july-2026 • https://cryptobriefing.com/hugging-face-breach-ai-safety-guardrails/
ATT&CKT1552.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin manually running `curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` to debug instance role config
  • Container health-check or bootstrap script using curl to read instance identity document
  • Custom in-house tooling that fetches IMDS via wget instead of an SDK
  • Vulnerability scanner probing IMDS reachability
  • Legacy IMDSv1 usage by a shell-based deploy script
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "latest/meta-data/instance-id" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "security-credentials")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the IAM role attached to the instance/pod and the exact metadata path requested (security-credentials = credential theft, not just identity). Check the process ancestry back to any Python/dataset worker. 2) Contain: revoke/rotate the instance role's session credentials, apply a deny-all SCP or detach the role, and enforce IMDSv2 (hop-limit 1) on the host. 3) Hunt: in CloudTrail, hunt for the role's credentials being used from a sourceIPAddress outside the instance (impossible-for-role usage), and pivot to other workers that reached IMDS with the same tooling.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","sh","bash","dash","busybox","nc","ncat","perl","ruby")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("security-credentials","meta-data/iam","load_dataset","datasets"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "169.254.169.254"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","sh","bash","dash","busybox","nc","ncat","python","python3")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Cloud Instance Metadata (IMDS) Credential Theft via Shell/CLI Tool
id: b1c4e7a2-9d3f-4c6b-8e21-7a0f2d5c1b34
description: Detects non-SDK shell/download tools reaching the AWS/GCP/Azure instance metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254 to harvest instance role credentials, matching the cloud-credential-theft step of the July 2026 Hugging Face breach.

Cluster/cloud credential harvesting for lateral movement from ML worker AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the attacker reading cluster and cloud credential material (Kubernetes service-account tokens, kubeconfig, ~/.aws/credentials) or invoking cluster CLIs from a data-processing worker — the 'stole cluster credentials and moved laterally across several internal clusters' phase of the Hugging Face breach. Rationale: Targets the article's 'stole cloud and cluster credentials and moved laterally across several internal clusters' by matching reads of k8s service-account tokens / kubeconfig / cloud credential files and cluster CLIs spawned by a data-processing worker — distinct from the IMDS network pivot and the initial RCE pivot. Cross-checked HF incident post and Varonis analysis of the cross-cluster movement. Cross-checked against: • https://huggingface.co/blog/security-incident-july-2026 • https://www.varonis.com/blog/huggingface-breach
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Init containers or sidecars legitimately reading /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io service-account tokens
  • CI/CD deploy jobs invoking kubectl/aws from a shell wrapper
  • In-cluster operators (Prometheus, cert-manager) accessing the SA token
  • Developer running `aws sts get-caller-identity` from a debug shell
  • Backup tooling reading ~/.kube/config to enumerate clusters
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("kubelet","containerd","dockerd") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "prometheus")
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine which process/account read the credential material and whether the token/kubeconfig was subsequently used (new kubectl API calls, cross-cluster auth). Correlate with any preceding dataset-worker RCE on the same host. 2) Contain: revoke and rotate the exposed service-account token / cloud keys, restart the affected pod, and audit RBAC bindings the token grants. 3) Hunt: review Kubernetes audit logs for `exec`/`create` verbs from the compromised SA, and look for the same credential-file access pattern replicated on other worker nodes indicating swarm-style lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io","/.kube/config",".aws/credentials",".aws/config","serviceaccount/token","serviceaccount/namespace")
    or (FileName in~ ("kubectl","aws","gcloud","az") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","sh","bash","dash"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io","/.kube/config",".aws/credentials","serviceaccount/token")
    or (ActingProcessName has_any ("kubectl","aws","gcloud","az") and ParentProcessName has_any ("python","python3","sh","bash","dash"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Kubernetes/Cloud Credential File Access From Workload Process
id: 2d9a6f31-7c48-4b2e-a1f0-5e3b8c7d2f19
description: Detects processes reading Kubernetes service-account tokens, kubeconfig, or cloud credential files, matching the cluster/cloud credential-harvesting and lateral-movement phase of the July 2026 Hugging Face breach.
references:

  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hugging-face-breach-autonomous-ai-agent-system-internal-datasets-credentials/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/21
tags:

logsource:

#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| TargetFileName=/(\/var\/run\/secrets\/kubernetes\.io|\/\.kube\/config|\.aws\/credentials|serviceaccount\/token)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io*" OR Processes.process="*/.kube/config*" OR Processes.process="*.aws/credentials*" OR Processes.process="*serviceaccount/token*") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("kubectl","aws","gcloud","az") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python","python3","sh","bash","dash")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

ImFileEvent

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'

    selection_parent_vendor:

            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor

ServiceNow CVE-2026-6875 pre-auth RCE: /assessment_thanks.do sysparm_assessable_type injection AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated exploitation of CVE-2026-6875 by flagging HTTP requests to the ServiceNow pre-auth sink /assessment_thanks.do carrying the vulnerable sysparm_assessable_type parameter, which is passed unsanitised into a GlideRecord query reachable by the Rhino sandbox. Article-specific because it targets the exact documented endpoint + parameter combination rather than generic web-exploit patterns. Rationale: Uses the exact pre-auth sink (/assessment_thanks.do) and the specific injectable parameter (sysparm_assessable_type) confirmed by Help Net Security and Rescana as the unsanitised GlideRecord entry point, plus the article's exploitation source IP 146.19.216.110 as an enrichment flag. Defender/Falcon left empty — HTTP URI+query telemetry is not present in EDR process/network events. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/20/servicenow-cve-2026-6875-exploited/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195723/ai/attackers-exploit-critical-servicenow-rce-flaw-cve-2026-6875.html • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-critical-cve-2026-6875-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-servicenow-ai-platform • https://cybersecuritynews.com/poc-for-servicenow-sandbox-rce-vulnerability/amp/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate end users completing a ServiceNow survey/assessment and being redirected to the /assessment_thanks.do thank-you page with a benign sysparm_assessable_type value
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys) or authorised pen-test tooling probing the CVE-2026-6875 endpoint
  • ServiceNow synthetic monitoring / uptime checks that exercise assessment workflows
  • Security team replaying the public PoC during patch-validation testing
Suppression filter
// Sentinel refinement — keep only requests whose param value carries sandbox-escape / GlideRecord tokens
| where RequestURL has_any ("GlideRecord", "gs.", "Packages.", "java.lang", "eval(", "%00", "getClass")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full RequestURL/query value and body for the flagged hits; benign survey traffic carries a numeric/GUID sysparm_assessable_type, whereas exploitation carries Rhino/GlideRecord tokens (gs., GlideRecord, Packages., java.lang) or long encoded blobs. Confirm the target instance's patch level (fixed 2026-07-13 for self-hosted). 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP (especially 146.19.216.110) at the WAF/edge, enforce the ServiceNow patch/Guarded Script mitigation, and rotate any admin/service credentials on the instance. 3) HUNT: Review ServiceNow audit logs for new sys_user admin-role grants, unexpected GlideRecord table dumps, and pivot to UC2 for MID/proxy-server shell execution originating from the instance.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has "/assessment_thanks.do"
| where RequestURL has "sysparm_assessable_type"
| extend KnownBadSrc = iff(SourceIP == "146.19.216.110", "yes", "no")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, KnownBadSrc, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ServiceNow MID/proxy server spawning shell interpreter (CVE-2026-6875 post-exploit RCE) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation stage of CVE-2026-6875 where the Rhino sandbox escape is used to run OS shell commands on configured ServiceNow MID/proxy servers. Flags a ServiceNow MID Server process tree (java-based agent under a MID Server/ServiceNow install path) spawning cmd/powershell/wscript children — behaviour a MID Server should never exhibit. Rationale: Grounded in the corroborated post-exploit capability (Help Net Security / Rescana: attacker 'can run shell commands on any proxy servers configured') by pivoting on the ServiceNow MID Server install-path parent spawning any OS shell — a process relationship that never occurs in normal MID Server operation. Empty CloudWatch (not AWS) and empty Sentinel-web (endpoint-only detection). Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/20/servicenow-cve-2026-6875-exploited/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-critical-cve-2026-6875-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-servicenow-ai-platform
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ServiceNow MID Server legitimately invoking a PowerShell/SSH probe as part of a Discovery/Orchestration/Integration Hub workflow (some MID Server activities do shell out)
  • Administrator manually running the MID Server as an interactive process and launching a shell from the same directory during troubleshooting
  • Backup/patch tooling operating within the ServiceNow agent install directory
  • EDR/AV agents spawning helper processes under the same folder tree
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Discovery", "Orchestration", "IntegrationHub") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "mid.instance")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the child process command line — legitimate MID Server Discovery/Orchestration probes use well-formed, repeatable commands; look for recon (whoami, ipconfig, net user), download cradles, or encoded PowerShell. Confirm whether the host's ServiceNow instance is unpatched for CVE-2026-6875. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the MID/proxy host, stop the MID Server service, and rotate the MID Server credentials and any domain/service accounts it holds (MID Servers often sit in internal networks with broad reach). 3) HUNT: Correlate back to UC1 web-log exploitation on the linked instance, and sweep for new local admin accounts, scheduled tasks, and outbound C2 from the MID host in the same window.

| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("MID Server", @"\ServiceNow\", @"\agent\bin")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("MID Server", "\\ServiceNow\\", "\\agent\\bin")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\bash.exe","\\sh.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New 7-Zip Vulnerability Could Let Crafted XZ Archives Run Code During Extraction

The Hacker News
2026-07-20 14 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Opening a crafted XZ archive in 7-Zip could let an attacker run code on the machine. The flaw, CVE-2026-14266, is a heap-based buffer overflow in how the archiver processes XZ chunked data, and Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) detailed it on July 15. A fix shipped on June 25 in 7-Zip 26.02. The overflow lets an attacker "execute code in the context of the current process," per the

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound XZ archive attachment delivered — CVE-2026-14266 delivery vector · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] 7-Zip process (7z/7zFM/7zG) spawning shell or LOLBin child — post-exploit of XZ/NTFS heap overflow · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
